result:
The museum opened at nine, though almost nobody came before eleven.

It occupied a former railway station in a town the trains no longer visited. Above the entrance, someone had removed the old destination board but left its frame. In winter, sparrows gathered inside it, arranging themselves into announcements.

The museum collected unfinished things.

There was a violin with only three strings, donated by a man who had intended to learn it after retirement. There was a half-knitted yellow sleeve. There were architectural drawings for a house whose proposed occupants had stopped speaking to one another halfway through the planning.

Each object had a small card explaining where the work had stopped.

*The sleeve was intended for a child who outgrew it.*

*The house was never built. The kitchen window would have faced east.*

In the largest room stood a wooden boat. Its builder had completed the hull and one oar before his eyesight began to fail. He had continued for several months by touch. Visitors sometimes ran a hand along the gunwale until the attendant asked them not to.

A boy named Emil came every Saturday because his mother cleaned the museum. He did his homework behind the ticket desk and ate sandwiches in the old luggage office.

One afternoon, he asked why there weren’t any unfinished sandwiches.

“They wouldn’t keep,” his mother said.

“So these are just unfinished things that don’t rot?”

She considered this while squeezing water from a mop.

“Mostly.”

For a school assignment, Emil had to describe an important institution in his community. He wrote about the museum. His teacher returned the paper with a note suggesting he explain what visitors could learn there.

The following Saturday, he carried the assignment from room to room. He looked at a jigsaw puzzle missing its border, a landscape painting with a blank white sky, and six pages of a novel about a dentist. He sat beside the boat for a long time.

Then he went back to the ticket desk and wrote:

*You can see how far people got.*

His teacher gave him a better mark.

Years later, when the museum lost its funding, Emil helped pack the collection. Most of it went to storage in a municipal basement. The boat was too large for the stairwell.

They carried it outside and set it on the platform while they decided what to do. Rain was coming. Someone fetched a tarpaulin; someone else went to measure a warehouse door.

Emil stood beside the hull, holding the single oar.

Across the tracks, beyond the weeds and rusted signal, the river passed through town. He had lived there all his life and had never noticed how easily a boat could be carried down to it.

He mentioned this to the others.

For a moment, nobody answered. Then the woman holding the tarpaulin folded it over her arm and said they ought to check whether the hull would float.
